claim: Homologous recombination-mediated repair behind a stalled replication fork can join the two nascent daughter chromosomes, resulting in a chromosome dimer.
source: In organisms with circular genomes, homologous recombination-mediated repair behind a stalled replication fork can join the two nascent daughter chromosomes, resulting in a chromosome dimer (Barre et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Barre et al., 2001.

claim: Dimer formation prohibits proper segregation of the genetic information at cell division.
source: Dimer formation prohibits proper segregation of the genetic information at cell division (Figure 1A), and must be repaired to produce viable progeny.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A which illustrates the role of Xer recombination in chromosome maintenance.

claim: In bacteria and archaea, chromosome dimers are monomerized by members of a large family of tyrosine recombinases, the Xer recombinases.
source: In bacteria and archaea, chromosome dimers are monomerized by members of a large family of tyrosine recombinases, the Xer recombinases (Blakely et al., 1991, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blakely et al., 1991, 1993.

claim: Xer recombinases act by promoting recombination between two DNA sites, called dif.
source: These enzymes act by promoting recombination between two DNA sites, called dif.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the mechanism of Xer recombinases, drawing from established knowledge in the field.

claim: The dif site is normally present in a single copy at the replication terminus.
source: The dif site is normally present in a single copy at the replication terminus (Carnoy and Roten, 2009; Kuempel et al., 1991), but it is duplicated in chromosome dimers, so that intramolecular recombination results in separation ('resolution') of the two chromosome copies (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Carnoy and Roten, 2009 and Kuempel et al., 1991, and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Removal of the xer genes or the dif site results in increased DNA content, activation of the SOS response, cell filamentation, and cell death.
source: Removal of the xer genes or the dif site results in increased DNA content, activation of the SOS response, cell filamentation, and cell death (Britton and Grossman, 1999; Debowski et al., 2012a; Hendricks et al., 2000; Pérals et al., 2000; Val et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Xer recombinases can support plasmid resolution and mobilization of the cholera toxin phage CTXϕ and pathogenicity islands.
source: Besides chromosome dimer resolution, Xer recombinases can support plasmid resolution and mobilization of the cholera toxin phage CTXϕ and pathogenicity islands (Das et al., 2013; Fischer et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Das et al., 2013 and Fischer et al., 2010.

claim: In E. coli, Xer recombination is carried out by cooperation of two similar enzymes XerC and XerD (37% identity).
source: In E. coli, Xer recombination is carried out by cooperation of two similar enzymes XerC and XerD (37% identity) that act together to bind and recombine dif sites (Blakely et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Blakely et al., 1993.

claim: Many organisms employ a single Xer recombinase system.
source: Many other organisms (including Lactococcus, Helicobacter, Campylobacter spp. and archaea) employ a single Xer recombinase system (Carnoy and Roten, 2009; Cortez et al., 2010; Debowski et al., 2012a; Le Bourgeois et al., 2007; Leroux et al., 2013), with a prime example, XerH/difH, found in Helicobacter pylori, a gastric pathogen implicated in peptic ulcer disease and gastric cancer.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies of different organisms.

claim: Xer recombinases are members of the tyrosine site-specific recombinase superfamily.
source: Xer recombinases are members of the tyrosine site-specific recombinase superfamily, a large group of enzymes that catalyze DNA breakage and rejoining using a conserved tyrosine nucleophile (Grindley et al., 2006; Guo et al., 1997; Midonet and Barre, 2014; Nunes-Düby et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to review articles and studies.

claim: Tyrosine recombinases catalyze DNA breakage and rejoining using a conserved tyrosine nucleophile.
source: Xer recombinases are members of the tyrosine site-specific recombinase superfamily, a large group of enzymes that catalyze DNA breakage and rejoining using a conserved tyrosine nucleophile (Grindley et al., 2006; Guo et al., 1997; Midonet and Barre, 2014; Nunes-Düby et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to review articles and studies.

claim: Tyrosine recombinases promote various programmed DNA rearrangements including the monomerization of phage, plasmid and chromosome multimers, resolution of hairpin telomeres, and the movement of virulence and antibiotic resistance carrying integrative mobile genetic elements.
source: Tyrosine recombinases promote various programmed DNA rearrangements including the monomerization of phage, plasmid and chromosome multimers, resolution of hairpin telomeres, and the movement of virulence and antibiotic resistance carrying integrative mobile genetic elements (including phages and transposons)(Grindley et al., 2006; Jayaram et al., 2015; Midonet and Barre, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Tyrosine recombinases provide powerful genetic engineering tools that are widely used to carry out mutagenesis and DNA insertion in eukaryotic chromosomes.
source: In addition, tyrosine recombinases (as exemplified by Cre and Flp) provide powerful genetic engineering tools that are widely used to carry out mutagenesis and DNA insertion in eukaryotic chromosomes (Nagy, 2000; Turan et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nagy, 2000 and Turan et al., 2011.

claim: Tyrosine recombinases share a common chemical mechanism that involves step-wise breakage and exchange of four DNA strands in pairs, proceeding through a characteristic four-way Holliday junction (HJ) DNA intermediate.
source: Tyrosine recombinases share a common chemical mechanism that involves step-wise breakage and exchange of four DNA strands in pairs, proceeding through a characteristic four-way Holliday junction (HJ) DNA intermediate (Figure 1B)(Gopaul and Duyne, 1999; Grindley et al., 2006; Holliday, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Tyrosine recombinases cut each DNA strand with a polarity creating a covalent 3' phosphotyrosyl protein-DNA linkage and a free 5' hydroxyl group.
source: They cut each DNA strand with a polarity creating a covalent 3' phosphotyrosyl protein-DNA linkage and a free 5' hydroxyl group.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the chemical mechanism, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: All DNA cleavage and rejoining reactions take place in an ordered protein-DNA synaptic complex, comprising four recombinase molecules holding the two recombination partner DNA molecules together.
source: All DNA cleavage and rejoining reactions take place in an ordered protein-DNA synaptic complex, comprising four recombinase molecules holding the two recombination partner DNA molecules together.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the mechanism, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: Xer recombination at dif requires an accessory factor, FtsK.
source: An unusual feature of Xer recombination at dif is that it requires an accessory factor, FtsK (Aussel et al., 2002; Debowski et al., 2012a; Le Bourgeois et al., 2007; Leroux et al., 2013; Nolivos et al., 2010; Steiner et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: FtsK is a DNA motor protein that localizes to the bacterial cell division septum.
source: This DNA motor protein localizes to the bacterial cell division septum and contributes to segregating the sister chromosomes into the daughter cells by translocating towards their replication termini.
evidence: This is a direct statement about FtsK function, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: FtsK contributes to segregating the sister chromosomes into the daughter cells by translocating towards their replication termini.
source: This DNA motor protein localizes to the bacterial cell division septum and contributes to segregating the sister chromosomes into the daughter cells by translocating towards their replication termini.
evidence: This is a direct statement about FtsK function, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: On chromosome dimers, FtsK stops at the Xer-bound dif sites and activates recombination, triggering resolution of the dimers to monomers.
source: On chromosome dimers, FtsK stops at the Xer-bound dif sites and activates recombination, triggering resolution of the dimers to monomers (Aussel et al., 2002; Grainge et al., 2011; May et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Without FtsK, Xer-dif synaptic complexes are formed, but do not lead to final recombination products.
source: Without FtsK, Xer-dif synaptic complexes are formed, but do not lead to final recombination products (Aussel et al., 2002; Diagne et al., 2014; Grainge et al., 2011; Zawadzki et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Regulation by FtsK is critical to ensure that Xer recombination takes place only in the correct spatial and temporal context – at the division septum, when genome replication has been completed.
source: Regulation by FtsK is critical to ensure that Xer recombination takes place only in the correct spatial and temporal context – at the division septum, when genome replication has been completed – thereby ensuring faithful genome segregation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known functions of FtsK and Xer recombination.

claim: The overall shape and DNA conformation of initially formed XerH-difH synaptic complexes is considerably different from those of other tyrosine recombinases, such as Cre-loxP.
source: Remarkably, the overall shape and DNA conformation of initially formed XerH-difH synaptic complexes is considerably different from those of other tyrosine recombinases, such as Cre-loxP that has served as a model system for the family.
evidence: This is a direct comparison based on the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The unanticipated conformation of the pre-cleavage synaptic complex suggests a possible model for why Xer proteins require external activation.
source: The unanticipated conformation of the pre-cleavage synaptic complex suggests a possible model for why Xer proteins require external activation, and in comparison with the post-cleavage complex structure provides clues for how FtsK might stimulate recombination activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and comparison between pre- and post-cleavage structures.

claim: The structures provide a resource to construct models for other Xer synaptic complexes, including that of the heterotetrameric E. coli XerC/D system.
source: Our structures provide a resource to construct models for other Xer synaptic complexes, including that of the heterotetrameric E. coli XerC/D system.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the utility of the structures presented.

claim: The XerH-difH synaptic complex structure shows a synaptic complex with two difH molecules and four XerH subunits.
source: The resulting 2.1 Å resolution structure (Figure 2B and Table 1) shows a synaptic complex with two difH molecules and four XerH subunits (Figure 2B, left panel).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: Each difH site interacts with two XerH molecules, one molecule (molecule A) binding to the left arm and one (molecule B) to the right arm.
source: Each difH site interacts with two XerH molecules, one molecule (molecule A) binding to the left arm and one (molecule B) to the right arm.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure.

claim: The complex has overall two-fold symmetry relating the two DNA molecules and the XerH molecules bound to them.
source: The complex has overall two-fold symmetry relating the two DNA molecules and the XerH molecules bound to them (i.e. molecules A and B to A' and B'; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The overall fold of each protein subunit resembles that of other tyrosine recombinases, comprising two mostly helical domains connected by a 7-aa linker.
source: The overall fold of each protein subunit resembles that of other tyrosine recombinases, comprising two mostly helical domains connected by a 7-aa linker (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2C, compared with known structures.

claim: The C-terminal helix αO protrudes from the body of each catalytic domain into a cleft on the surface of an adjacent subunit in a cyclic fashion, creating a cyclic domain-swapped arrangement similar to the ones observed in the structures of Cre and λ integrase synaptic complexes.
source: Notably, the C-terminal helix αO protrudes from the body of each catalytic domain into a cleft on the surface of an adjacent subunit in a cyclic fashion, creating a cyclic domain-swapped arrangement similar to the ones observed in the structures of Cre (Figure 2B, right panel) and λ integrase synaptic complexes (Biswas et al., 2005; Guo et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure, compared with cited structures.

claim: The arrangement of the subunits within the synaptic complex differs from that observed previously, forming a considerably less compact synaptic interface with a wide open central channel.
source: Whereas the structure of individual XerH subunits is similar to that of other tyrosine recombinases, the arrangement of the subunits within the synaptic complex differs from that observed previously, forming a considerably less compact synaptic interface with a wide open central channel (illustrated by comparison with the 'paradigm' Cre-loxP structure in Figure 2B) (Guo et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a direct comparison based on the structural data shown in Figure 2B and cited structures.

claim: The DNA molecules assume a near-straight conformation, in contrast to all previously reported tyrosine recombinase synaptic complexes.
source: Furthermore, the DNA molecules assume a near-straight conformation, in contrast to all previously reported tyrosine recombinase synaptic complexes.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure, compared with known structures.

claim: The two domains of each subunit form a tight, C-shaped clamp around one arm of the difH site.
source: The two domains of each subunit form a tight, C-shaped clamp around one arm of the difH site (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The N-terminal domain contacts the DNA using a four-helix bundle (αA-αD, aa 12–88) and helix αF, both of which insert into the major groove.
source: The N-terminal domain contacts the DNA using a four-helix bundle (αA-αD, aa 12–88) and helix αF, both of which insert into the major groove (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The N-terminal domain protein segments contribute most of the sequence-specific interactions to the DNA bases, while the catalytic domain contacts mainly the DNA backbone.
source: These protein segments contribute most of the sequence-specific interactions to the DNA bases, while the catalytic domain contacts mainly the DNA backbone (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Helix αK (aa 285–299) is inserted into the major groove at the outer part of difH, narrows the groove (17 Å as opposed to 22 Å in typical B-DNA) and induces a slight DNA bend.
source: Many interactions of the catalytic domain involve helix αK (aa 285–299) that is inserted into the major groove at the outer part of difH, narrows the groove (17 Å as opposed to 22 Å in typical B-DNA) and induces a slight DNA bend (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2C.

claim: XerH covers 11 bp of the left difH arm and 10 bp of the right arm.
source: XerH covers 11 bp of the left difH arm and 10 bp of the right arm (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The inner 5 bp of each arm (positions 7–11 and 20–24) are recognized sequence-specifically.
source: The inner 5 bp of each arm (positions 7–11 and 20–24, Figure 2A) are recognized sequence-specifically (Figure 2D), while the outer nucleotides (positions 2–4 and 26–28) are mostly contacted at the phosphate backbone.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2A.

claim: Mutations of the inner base-pairs of the arms resulted in abolished or greatly reduced cleavage activity, whereas mutations of the neighboring base-pairs did not affect the activity.
source: As predicted by the structure, mutations of the inner base-pairs of the arms (where XerH makes base-specific contacts) resulted in abolished or greatly reduced cleavage activity, whereas mutations of the neighboring base-pairs did not affect the activity.
evidence: This is supported by cleavage assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Two XerH monomers bind cooperatively to one difH site.
source: DNA binding assays (EMSA) with substrates containing the sequences of one or both arms (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showed that two XerH monomers bind cooperatively (see especially Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The affinity of a difHL substrate containing only the left arm sequence was higher (KD = 180 nM; similar to wild-type difH KD = 150 nM) than the affinity of a similar right arm-containing substrate difHR (KD = 230 nM).
source: The affinity of a difHL substrate containing only the left arm sequence, with a random sequence in place of the right arm, was higher (dissociation constant, KD = 180 nM; similar to wild-type difH KD = 150 nM) than the affinity of a similar right arm-containing substrate difHR (KD = 230 nM).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A palindromic substrate containing two difH left arms (difHLP) made a stable complex with XerH, whereas the equivalent right arm substrate (difHRP) did not.
source: Similarly, a palindromic substrate containing two difH left arms (difHLP) made a stable complex with XerH (observed by SEC), whereas the equivalent right arm substrate (difHRP) did not (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No cleavage product was detected with difHR or difHRP, whereas difHL and difHLP substrates were cleaved as efficiently as the native difH site.
source: DNA cleavage assays also revealed different efficiencies at the two arms: no cleavage product was detected with difHR or difHRP, whereas difHL and difHLP substrates were cleaved as efficiently as the native difH site (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The wild-type recombination rate (9.9% recombination-positive colonies) increased when both difH sites were replaced with difHLP (29.4%; p=0.0016, t-test), but decreased to barely detectable levels with difHRP (1.3%; p=0.0021, t-test).
source: An assay that assesses the efficiency of intramolecular recombination between two plasmid-borne sites in E. coli also indicated differential activity at the two difH arms in vivo: the wild-type recombination rate (9.9% recombination-positive colonies) increased when both difH sites were replaced with difHLP (29.4%; p=0.0016, t-test), but decreased to barely detectable levels with difHRP (1.3%; p=0.0021, t-test) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo recombination assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The sequences of the two arms are identical apart from a single base-pair insertion in the left arm.
source: Remarkably, the sequences of the two arms are identical apart from a single base-pair insertion in the left arm (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the sequence shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The inserted base-pair (A6/T25', brown in Figure 2A) is not recognized directly.
source: The inserted base-pair (A6/T25', brown in Figure 2A) is not recognized directly.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure.

claim: In the left arm, T4 forms hydrophobic contacts with XerH αK and makes a specific hydrogen bond with lysine K290, whereas in the right arm T5' is closer to the center of difH and cannot make these interactions.
source: Instead, the main difference in the recognition of the two arms involves a conserved thymine base (T4/T5') in the outer parts of the arms: In the left arm, T4 forms hydrophobic contacts with XerH αK and makes a specific hydrogen bond with lysine K290 (Figure 3F, red insert), whereas in the right arm T5' is closer to the center of difH and cannot make these interactions.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The three outermost base-pairs of each difH arm make very similar backbone interactions with their respective XerH subunits, despite the fact that they are shifted in space due to the insertion in the left arm.
source: Surprisingly, the three outermost base-pairs of each difH arm make very similar backbone interactions with their respective XerH subunits, despite the fact that they are shifted in space due to the insertion in the left arm (altering the 'helical phase' of the sequence by ~35°; Figure 3F, black insert; Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 3F and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The conformation of the DNA is asymmetric – the left arm is more bent than the right arm – and the catalytic domains of the protein subunits are rotated by ~10° relative to each other.
source: This is possible because the conformation of the DNA is asymmetric – the left arm is more bent than the right arm – and the catalytic domains of the protein subunits are rotated by ~10° relative to each other (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The observed differences result in stronger interaction of XerH with the left difH arm (ΔG = −21.3 kcal/mol) than with the right arm (ΔG = −15.4 kcal/mol).
source: Together, the observed differences result in stronger interaction of XerH with the left difH arm (ΔG = −21.3 kcal/mol, estimated by PISA [Krissinel and Henrick, 2007]) than with the right arm (ΔG = −15.4 kcal/mol).
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure using PISA.

claim: While the αN-αO segment of molecule A is fully ordered, the linker and αO are partially disordered in molecule B.
source: A further difference between the XerH subunits bound to the left and right arms of difH concerns the C-terminal helices. While the αN-αO segment of molecule A is fully ordered, the linker and αO are partially disordered in molecule B.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure.

claim: Helices αO point in different directions (~100° rotation).
source: Also, helices αO point in different directions (~100° rotation; Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 3F.

claim: difH variants containing mutations at the inserted base-pair showed no or only moderate decreases in cleavage in vitro and recombination in vivo.
source: In agreement with the structure, difH variants containing mutations at the inserted base-pair showed no or only moderate decreases in cleavage in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) and recombination in vivo (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by cleavage and recombination assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: Substitutions of T4 practically abolished recombination in E. coli and in H. pylori.
source: In contrast, substitutions of T4 practically abolished recombination in E. coli (Figure 3E) and in H. pylori (Debowski et al., 2012a); and mutation of K290 (K290S) decreased recombination activity by about half (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by recombination assay data shown in Figure 3E and cited data from Debowski et al., 2012a.

claim: Mutation of K290 (K290S) decreased recombination activity by about half.
source: In contrast, substitutions of T4 practically abolished recombination in E. coli (Figure 3E) and in H. pylori (Debowski et al., 2012a); and mutation of K290 (K290S) decreased recombination activity by about half (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by recombination assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Insertion of an additional base-pair next to A6/T25' in the left arm abolished cleavage completely.
source: Insertion of an additional base-pair next to A6/T25' in the left arm, further shifting the positions of the three outermost base-pairs, also abolished cleavage completely (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: XerH does not contact the nucleotides flanking the left and right cleavage sites (positions C13 and G13').
source: However, XerH does not contact these nucleotides in our structure, and cleavage assays with difH variants carrying mutations at these positions revealed no reduction in activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), suggesting that the identity of these nucleotides does not contribute to XerH binding and cleavage asymmetry.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and cleavage assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: XerH binds preferentially to the left arm of difH thanks to favorable interactions with its outer sequence (including T4).
source: Together, these data demonstrate that XerH binds preferentially to the left arm of difH thanks to favorable interactions with its outer sequence (including T4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and biochemical data presented.

claim: Asymmetric interactions with the two arms of difH dictate distinct protein conformations in the synaptic complex, including differential positioning of the αN-αO segment that carries the nucleophilic tyrosine, perhaps helping to define which arm is cleaved first.
source: Asymmetric interactions with the two arms of difH also appear to dictate distinct protein conformations in the synaptic complex, including differential positioning of the αN-αO segment that carries the nucleophilic tyrosine, perhaps helping to define which arm is cleaved first.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: Both DNA molecules in the synapse resemble B-form DNA, with a wide angle (165°) between the two difH arms.
source: Both DNA molecules in the synapse resemble B-form DNA, with a wide angle (165°) between the two difH arms (Figure 2B, left panel).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The loxP DNA is bent to ~100° in the analogous pre-cleavage structures of Cre-loxP complexes.
source: For example, the loxP DNA is bent to ~100° in the analogous pre-cleavage structures of Cre-loxP complexes (Figure 2B, right panel).
evidence: This is a comparison with known structures shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In the active site of each XerH subunit, several conserved residues including the catalytic tyrosine Y344, two arginine (R213 and R312), and two histidine (H309 and H335) residues are assembled around the scissile phosphate.
source: In the active site of each XerH subunit, several conserved residues including the catalytic tyrosine Y344, two arginine (R213 and R312), and two histidine (H309 and H335) residues are assembled around the scissile phosphate, together forming a catalytic pocket characteristic of tyrosine recombinases.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure.

claim: The active sites of the subunits are very similar, except for the R213 side chain which points in different directions in molecules A and B.
source: The active sites of the subunits are very similar, except for the R213 side chain which points in different directions in molecules A and B (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Electron density for another essential catalytic residue, K239, could not be observed in either of the subunits, so it is presumed to be disordered.
source: Electron density for another essential catalytic residue, K239, could not be observed in either of the subunits, so we presume that it is disordered.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure.

claim: The catalytic tyrosine Y344 is far away (5.2–5.8 Å) from the scissile phosphate in all subunits, so the structure represents a catalytically inactive synaptic complex.
source: The catalytic tyrosine Y344 is far away (5.2–5.8 Å) from the scissile phosphate in all subunits, so the structure represents a catalytically inactive synaptic complex, implying a conformational change is required prior to catalysis.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure.

claim: The post-cleavage structure differs considerably from the pre-cleavage structure.
source: The resulting structure (Figure 4A) differs considerably from the pre-cleavage structure.
evidence: This is a direct comparison between the two structures shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the post-cleavage structure, the two halves of the tetramer are related by crystallographic two-fold symmetry.
source: Each difHLP site interacts with two XerH molecules in a tetrameric synaptic complex, but in this structure, the two halves of the tetramer are related by crystallographic two-fold symmetry (relating molecule A to A' and B to B'; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The difH DNA is strongly bent in the post-cleavage structure.
source: Most strikingly, the difH DNA is now strongly bent (Figure 4B, Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 4B and Video 1.

claim: The bend mainly originates from a single distortion within the central region of difH: bases A17' and G18' are un-stacked with a 90° tilt, which introduces a kink resulting in asymmetric bending of the DNA.
source: The bend mainly originates from a single distortion within the central region of difH: bases A17' and G18' are un-stacked with a 90° tilt, which introduces a kink resulting in asymmetric bending of the DNA (insert in Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The total angle of 120° between the difH arms is only slightly wider than the angles observed in previous structures of various tyrosine recombinases.
source: The total angle of 120° between the difH arms is only slightly wider than the angles observed in previous structures of various tyrosine recombinases (e.g. 109° in the post-cleavage structure of λ integrase (Biswas et al., 2005) and 100° in Cre-loxP (Guo et al., 1997); see also Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct comparison with cited structures.

claim: The kink in difH is at an equivalent position to the kink in loxP.
source: Notably, the kink in difH is at an equivalent position to the kink in loxP (Ennifar et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a comparison with cited structures.

claim: In Cre, the nucleotides involved in the kink interact with three arginines within a tight pocket, whereas XerH forms only a single interaction with these nucleotides (R129-A17') and encircles the kink less tightly.
source: However, whereas in Cre the nucleotides involved in the kink interact with three arginines within a tight pocket (Figure 4C) (Ennifar et al., 2003; Guo et al., 1997), XerH forms only a single interaction with these nucleotides (R129-A17'; Figure 4C; Figure 2—figure supplement 4A) and encircles the kink less tightly.
evidence: This is a direct comparison between the XerH structure and cited Cre structures shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The nucleotides of the central region of difH remain fully base-paired after cleavage, unlike the analogous structure of Cre-loxP, where several of these are unpaired.
source: Notably, the nucleotides of the central region of difH remain fully base-paired after cleavage, unlike the analogous structure of Cre-loxP, where several of these are unpaired (Guo et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a direct comparison with cited Cre-loxP structures.

claim: Extensive Cre contacts can actively bend loxP, whereas weaker XerH-difH interactions appear to be insufficient to promote sharp DNA bending.
source: The extensive Cre contacts can thus actively bend loxP. In contrast, weaker XerH-difH interactions appear to be insufficient to promote sharp DNA bending, but nicks in both DNA strands of the difH substrate facilitate bending.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural comparison and the observation that nicked substrates were used.

claim: Nicks in both DNA strands of the difH substrate facilitate bending.
source: The extensive Cre contacts can thus actively bend loxP. In contrast, weaker XerH-difH interactions appear to be insufficient to promote sharp DNA bending, but nicks in both DNA strands of the difH substrate facilitate bending.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and the use of nicked substrates.

claim: When the DNA strands in the post-cleavage structure were re-built to model a bent but un-nicked substrate, a clash with the protein near the tyrosine nucleophile-bearing helix αN was observed, suggesting that the nicks might favor the XerH conformation adopted on the bent sites.
source: When we tried to re-build the DNA strands in the post-cleavage structure to model a bent but un-nicked substrate, we observed a clash with the protein near the tyrosine nucleophile-bearing helix αN, suggesting that the nicks might favor the XerH conformation adopted on the bent sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on molecular modeling.

claim: Each subunit is rotated by ~22° in the post-cleavage structure, resulting in major rewiring of the inter-subunit interactions and an overall compaction of the complex.
source: The arrangement of the XerH subunits is also markedly different in the two structures. Each subunit is rotated by ~22° in the post-cleavage structure (Figure 4B, Video 1), resulting in major rewiring of the inter-subunit interactions and an overall compaction of the complex.
evidence: This is a direct comparison between the two structures shown in Figure 4B and Video 1.

claim: The synaptic interface is considerably larger (3926 Å2) in the post-cleavage structure than in the pre-cleavage structure (3040 Å2).
source: Also, the synaptic interface is considerably larger (3926 Å2, calculated by PISA [Krissinel and Henrick, 2007]) than in the pre-cleavage structure (3040 Å2).
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structures using PISA.

claim: The previously disordered parts of the αO helices of molecule B are now fully visible, ordered, and more compact in the post-cleavage structure.
source: The previously disordered parts of the αO helices of molecule B are now fully visible, ordered, and more compact (F338 - W359 distance reduced from 43 Å to 34 Å; Figure 4D, left insert).
evidence: This is a direct comparison between the two structures shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Helices αN and αO of molecule A are rotated by ~30° in the post-cleavage structure, bringing the catalytic Y344 to a suitable position to attack one strand on each difHLP DNA forming a covalent phosphotyrosyl bond.
source: At the same time, helices αN and αO of molecule A are rotated by ~30°, bringing the catalytic Y344 to a suitable position to attack one strand on each difHLP DNA forming a covalent phosphotyrosyl bond (Figure 4E, left).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Despite the symmetry of the palindromic difHLP substrate, the two bound XerH molecules (A and B) are in different conformations.
source: Interestingly, despite the symmetry of the palindromic difHLP substrate, the two bound XerH molecules (A and B) are in different conformations (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Subunit A assumes a fully active conformation, while subunit B is in an inactive conformation with the catalytic tyrosine distant from the scissile phosphate.
source: Consequently, subunit A assumes a fully active conformation, while subunit B is in an inactive conformation with the catalytic tyrosine distant from the scissile phosphate (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The simultaneous presence of both active and inactive XerH subunit conformations within the synaptic complex is consistent with the 'half-of-the-sites reactivity' mechanism observed for other tyrosine recombinases.
source: This simultaneous presence of both active and inactive XerH subunit conformations within the synaptic complex is consistent with the 'half-of-the-sites reactivity' mechanism observed for other tyrosine recombinases (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and comparison with known mechanisms.

claim: The marked difference between the XerH subunits bound to the two difHLP arms is particularly striking considering that the artificially introduced symmetry of the substrate could be expected to mask some asymmetric features of the synaptic complex.
source: The marked difference between the XerH subunits bound to the two difHLP arms (comparable to the asymmetry seen in the pre-cleavage complex with native difH) is particularly striking considering that the artificially introduced symmetry of the substrate could be expected to mask some asymmetric features of the synaptic complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: The asymmetry is presumably an intrinsic property of the system, essential to the mechanism of synapsis and catalysis.
source: The asymmetry is presumably an intrinsic property of the system, essential to the mechanism of synapsis and catalysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: Due to high structural conservation within the Xer family, the XerH structures can provide insights into the mechanisms of other Xer recombinases.
source: Due to high structural conservation within the Xer family (Subramanya et al., 1997) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), our XerH structures can provide insights into the mechanisms of other Xer recombinases that have eluded structural studies so far.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and cited structural data.

claim: The models place XerC on the right arm of difH and XerD on the left arm.
source: Our models place XerC on the right arm of difH and XerD on the left arm.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the modeling approach.

claim: The observation that XerH preferentially cleaves at the left arm of difH first supports the hypothesis that the XerH subunit on the left arm corresponds to XerD whereas the subunit on the right arm corresponds to XerC.
source: We cannot exclude the alternative assignment, but our observation that XerH preferentially cleaves at the left arm of difH first (Figure 3D) supports the hypothesis that the XerH subunit on the left arm corresponds to XerD whereas the subunit on the right arm corresponds to XerC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cleavage data shown in Figure 3D and analogy with the XerC/D system.

claim: In the models, the XerC and XerD monomers each form C-shaped clamps around one arm of the dif site.
source: In the models, the XerC and XerD monomers each form C-shaped clamps around one arm of the dif site (Figure 5B), and make multiple sequence-specific and backbone interactions with the DNA.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the models shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The five conserved catalytic residues (RHRHY) assemble around the catalytic pocket in all XerC and XerD subunits.
source: The five conserved catalytic residues (RHRHY) assemble around the catalytic pocket in all XerC and XerD subunits (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the models shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the post-cleavage complex model, the XerD subunits are in an active conformation, with their nucleophilic tyrosines approaching the scissile phosphates, whereas the XerC subunits are in an inactive conformation.
source: In the post-cleavage complex, the XerD subunits are in an active conformation, with their nucleophilic tyrosines approaching the scissile phosphates, whereas the XerC subunits are in an inactive conformation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the models.

claim: The three outer base-pairs of each dif arm are contacted extensively by the proteins in the models, and the bases corresponding to T4 in difH interact with lysine K222 of XerC or histidine H225 of XerD.
source: As in the XerH structures, the three outer base-pairs of each dif arm are contacted extensively by the proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), and the bases corresponding to T4 in difH interact with lysine K222 of XerC or histidine H225 of XerD, both counterparts of XerH K290 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the models shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: These interactions might contribute to the arm specificity of XerC and XerD, as well as to ordering recombination.
source: These interactions might contribute to the arm specificity of XerC and XerD, as well as to ordering recombination, as we inferred for XerH.
evidence: This is an inference based on the models and analogy with XerH.

claim: The interactions involved in DNA kinking in Cre are absent in the XerC/D-dif complex, suggesting that these enzymes, like XerH, might be unable to independently initiate sharp DNA bending.
source: The interactions involved in DNA kinking in Cre are absent in the XerC/D-dif complex, suggesting that these enzymes, like XerH, might be unable to independently initiate sharp DNA bending.
evidence: This is an inference based on the models and comparison with Cre.

claim: The protein arrangements and interfaces observed in the two XerH-difH structures are well accommodated by XerC and XerD.
source: The protein arrangements and interfaces observed in our two XerH-difH structures are well accommodated by XerC and XerD, the pre-cleavage model showing nearly straight DNA and the post-cleavage model containing bent DNA and tightened intersubunit interactions (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the models shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The XerC/D and XerH complexes might undergo similar conformational rearrangements upon activation.
source: This suggests that the XerC/D and XerH complexes might undergo similar conformational rearrangements upon activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the models.

claim: Two previous smFRET studies reported that pre-formed XerC/D-dif synaptic complexes undergo conformational change upon activation by FtsK, leading to an increase of the distance between the two dif termini from about 53 to 67 Å across the synapse.
source: In agreement with this idea, two previous smFRET studies (Diagne et al., 2014; Zawadzki et al., 2013) reported that pre-formed XerC/D-dif synaptic complexes undergo conformational change upon activation by FtsK, leading to an increase of the distance between the two dif termini from about 53 to 67 Å across the synapse (as predicted from a change in FRET efficiencies; [Zawadzki et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to smFRET studies.

claim: The XerC/D-dif models predict a similar change from 46 Å in the pre-cleavage state to 60 Å in the post-cleavage state.
source: Our XerC/D-dif models predict a similar change from 46 Å in the pre-cleavage state to 60 Å in the post-cleavage state.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the models and comparison with smFRET data.

claim: Xer proteins follow the established chemical pathway of tyrosine recombinases.
source: These structures demonstrate that Xer proteins follow the established chemical pathway of tyrosine recombinases and reveal how the reaction steps can be choreographed by small differences in the arms of the difH recombination sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: The reaction steps can be choreographed by small differences in the arms of the difH recombination sites.
source: These structures demonstrate that Xer proteins follow the established chemical pathway of tyrosine recombinases and reveal how the reaction steps can be choreographed by small differences in the arms of the difH recombination sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: XerH-difH synaptic complexes initially assemble in an inactive state with straight DNA, which must undergo a major conformational change for catalytic activation.
source: Together with associated biochemical data, the structures also show that XerH-difH synaptic complexes initially assemble in an inactive state with straight DNA, which must undergo a major conformational change for catalytic activation, as previously observed in single molecule fluorescence studies of XerC/D-dif recombination (Diagne et al., 2014; Zawadzki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and biochemical data, supported by citations to smFRET studies.

claim: The post-cleavage XerH-difH synaptic complex structure elucidates the structural nature of the conformational change, which involves major rearrangement of the protein-protein interfaces and DNA bending.
source: Our post-cleavage XerH-difH synaptic complex structure elucidates the structural nature of this conformational change, which involves major rearrangement of the protein-protein interfaces and DNA bending (Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the structural data shown in Video 1.

claim: The structures provide a resource for understanding the mechanism of other Xer recombinases.
source: With molecular modeling, we extend our structural and mechanistic findings to the prototypical E. coli XerC/D-dif system, demonstrating that our structures provide a resource for understanding the mechanism of other Xer recombinases.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the utility of the structures.

claim: The recombination process starts with XerH binding to the difH site on the H. pylori chromosome.
source: The recombination process starts with XerH binding to the difH site on the H. pylori chromosome (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proposed mechanism shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Two XerH subunits bind cooperatively to one difH site.
source: Two XerH subunits bind cooperatively to one difH site (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 6A), each forming a clamp around one arm of difH (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and structural data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 6A.

claim: The difH left arm has higher affinity for XerH than the right arm, leading to the second XerH molecule binding to the right arm more often than vice versa.
source: The difH left arm has higher affinity for XerH than the right arm (Figure 3A,B), leading to the second XerH molecule binding to the right arm more often than vice versa.
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Cooperative binding of XerH involves extensive contacts between the two subunits bound to each difH.
source: Cooperative binding of XerH involves extensive contacts between the two subunits bound to each difH, as revealed by our structures (1650.6 Å2 surface area with ΔG = −12.6 kcal/mol and 1515.5 Å2 with ΔG = −14.5 kcal/mol between molecules A-B and A'-B' respectively in the pre-cleavage structure; and 1379.8 Å2 surface area with ΔG of −13.8 kcal/mol in the post-cleavage structure).
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structures.

claim: Despite the near-perfect dyad symmetry of the difH arms, the bound XerH subunits are structurally distinct.
source: Despite the near-perfect dyad symmetry of the difH arms, the bound XerH subunits are structurally distinct.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure.

claim: The left arm subunit assumes a conformation primed for DNA cleavage, whereas the right arm subunit is forced in an inactive state.
source: The left arm subunit assumes a conformation primed for DNA cleavage, whereas the right arm subunit is forced in an inactive state.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure.

claim: This asymmetric configuration defines the order of all subsequent cleavage and strand transfer events.
source: This asymmetric configuration defines the order of all subsequent cleavage and strand transfer events.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: Two XerH-bound difH sites interact to create a tetrameric synaptic complex.
source: Two XerH-bound difH sites then interact to create a tetrameric synaptic complex, as we see in our crystal structures (Figure 2B; Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structures shown in Figure 2B and Figure 6B.

claim: The sites align in antiparallel, and intersubunit interactions across the synaptic interface anchor the αO helices of the right arm-bound XerH subunits on their left arm-bound partner, creating a 'circular' domain-swapped arrangement.
source: The sites align in antiparallel, and intersubunit interactions across the synaptic interface anchor the αO helices of the right arm-bound XerH subunits on their left arm-bound partner, creating a 'circular' domain-swapped arrangement, similar to the ones described for other tyrosine recombinases such as Cre and λ integrase (Biswas et al., 2005; Guo et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure, compared with cited structures.

claim: The pre-cleavage synaptic complex crystal structure contains nearly straight difH DNA, and XerH is in a catalytically inactive conformation.
source: The pre-cleavage synaptic complex crystal structure contains nearly straight difH DNA (Figure 2B; Figure 6B), and XerH is in a catalytically inactive conformation (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structures shown in Figure 2B, Figure 3G, and Figure 6B.

claim: XerH was unable to observe difH recombination or XerH-mediated cleavage of intact difH DNA substrates in vitro.
source: Correspondingly, we were unable to observe difH recombination or XerH-mediated cleavage of intact difH DNA substrates in vitro (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by cleavage assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nicked difH suicide substrates are cleaved efficiently.
source: In contrast, nicked difH suicide substrates are cleaved efficiently, and our crystal structure in which XerH-mediated cleavage of nicked difH has occurred showed a sharply bent DNA conformation, consistent with a direct link between DNA bending and cleavage activity.
evidence: This is supported by cleavage assay data and the post-cleavage crystal structure.

claim: The crystal structure in which XerH-mediated cleavage of nicked difH has occurred showed a sharply bent DNA conformation, consistent with a direct link between DNA bending and cleavage activity.
source: In contrast, nicked difH suicide substrates are cleaved efficiently, and our crystal structure in which XerH-mediated cleavage of nicked difH has occurred showed a sharply bent DNA conformation, consistent with a direct link between DNA bending and cleavage activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: The in vitro systems lack a stimulatory factor that is required for normal recombination between intact difH sites.
source: We hypothesize that our in vitro systems lack a stimulatory factor that is required for normal recombination between intact difH sites.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the inability to observe recombination in vitro.

claim: Septum-borne FtsK is required for XerH recombination in H. pylori.
source: Septum-borne FtsK was shown to be required for XerH recombination in H. pylori (Debowski et al., 2012a), so we propose that this is the missing factor for XerH activation in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Debowski et al., 2012a.

claim: FtsK-promoted rearrangement of the XerH-difH synaptic complex might bring the catalytic tyrosines of the left arm-bound subunits into their active positions close to the scissile phosphates and sharply bend the DNA.
source: FtsK-promoted rearrangement of the XerH-difH synaptic complex might bring the catalytic tyrosines of the left arm-bound subunits into their active positions close to the scissile phosphates and sharply bend the DNA as seen in our structures (Figures 4B and 6C; Video 1).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural data shown in Figures 4B, 6C, and Video 1.

claim: FtsK might mediate formation of a different synaptic complex with the right arm-bound subunits activated for cleavage, but this would be inconsistent with smFRET studies of XerC/D complexes showing that FtsK activates pre-formed synaptic complexes without major remodeling.
source: Another possibility is that FtsK mediates formation of a different synaptic complex with the right arm-bound subunits activated for cleavage. However, this would be inconsistent with smFRET studies of XerC/D complexes showing that FtsK activates pre-formed synaptic complexes without major remodeling (Zawadzki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation that is evaluated against cited smFRET data.

claim: Analogy with the XerC/D system suggests that FtsK might directly interact with the C-terminal ~20 amino acids of XerH or the back of its C-terminal domain.
source: Analogy with the XerC/D system suggests that FtsK might directly interact with the C-terminal ~20 amino acids of XerH (Yates et al., 2006) or the back of its C-terminal domain (Keller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation based on analogy with the XerC/D system and cited studies.

claim: The role of FtsK in the H. pylori Xer system still requires further substantial investigation.
source: However, the role of FtsK in the H. pylori Xer system still requires further substantial investigation, and it remains possible that the bent-DNA configuration required for DNA cleavage can be reached from the pre-cleavage structure without the intervention of FtsK.
evidence: This is a direct statement acknowledging the limitations of the current study.

claim: Following activation, XerH-catalysed DNA strand cleavage and rejoining presumably follow the conserved tyrosine recombination pathway, with the XerH subunits bound to the left arms performing the first strand exchanges.
source: Following activation, XerH-catalysed DNA strand cleavage and rejoining presumably follow the conserved tyrosine recombination pathway (Figure 1B), with the XerH subunits bound to the left arms performing the first strand exchanges.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and known mechanisms shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The resulting HJ is then resolved by a reciprocal set of chemical reactions catalysed by the XerH subunits bound to the right arms.
source: The resulting HJ is then resolved by a reciprocal set of chemical reactions catalysed by the XerH subunits bound to the right arms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known mechanism of tyrosine recombinases.

claim: DNA bending is a prerequisite for activity of many molecular machines, including transcription factors, topoisomerases and recombinases.
source: DNA bending is a prerequisite for activity of many molecular machines, including transcription factors, topoisomerases and recombinases (Dong and Berger, 2007; Kim et al., 1993; Lee et al., 2013; Yang and Steitz, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of various molecular machines.

claim: For tyrosine recombinases, the paradigm suggests that sharp DNA bending that is required for DNA cleavage and energetically inexpensive strand exchange, is introduced by the recombinase itself concomitant with DNA binding and synapsis.
source: For tyrosine recombinases, the paradigm suggests that sharp DNA bending that is required for DNA cleavage and energetically inexpensive strand exchange, is introduced by the recombinase itself concomitant with DNA binding and synapsis.
evidence: This is a statement about the established paradigm in the field.

claim: XerH binds and assembles its recombination substrates in an almost straight conformation.
source: Here, we show that this is not the case for XerH, which binds and assembles its recombination substrates in an almost straight conformation.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the crystal structure.

claim: The required DNA bending presumably occurs upon activation by an external factor that is present only in a particular spatial and temporal context, providing an elegant regulatory mechanism to ensure faithful chromosome segregation.
source: The required DNA bending then presumably occurs upon activation by an external factor that is present only in a particular spatial and temporal context, providing an elegant regulatory mechanism to ensure faithful chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and the known requirement for FtsK.

claim: The architectures of the pre- and post- cleavage synaptic complexes are probably conserved between XerC/D and XerH.
source: Our modeling of XerC/D-dif indicates that the architectures of the pre- and post- cleavage synaptic complexes are probably conserved between XerC/D and XerH (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the models shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The DNA conformational changes observed for XerH-difH are consistent with smFRET studies of XerC/D-dif synaptic complexes.
source: The DNA conformational changes that we observe for XerH-difH are also consistent with smFRET studies of XerC/D-dif synaptic complexes (Diagne et al., 2014; Zawadzki et al., 2013), which imply a conformational change upon FtsK-mediated activation consistent with the differences between our models of the pre-cleavage and post-cleavage complexes.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with cited smFRET studies.

claim: The mechanism of catalytic activation proposed for XerH – preassembly of a synaptic complex with almost straight DNA, followed by FtsK-induced protein and DNA rearrangements activating the complex for catalysis – may be conserved in the XerC/D system.
source: Thus, we expect that the mechanism of catalytic activation proposed here for XerH – preassembly of a synaptic complex with almost straight DNA, followed by FtsK-induced protein and DNA rearrangements activating the complex for catalysis – may be conserved in the XerC/D system.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural data and modeling.

claim: Catalysis by the Xer family of site-specific recombination systems follows the established tyrosine recombinase pathway, with the reaction steps being choreographed by small differences in the arms of the dif recombination sites.
source: In summary, our structures of XerH-difH complexes demonstrate that catalysis by the Xer family of site-specific recombination systems follows the established tyrosine recombinase pathway, with the reaction steps being choreographed by small differences in the arms of the dif recombination sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: Contrary to previous assumption, bending of the dif sites does not occur concomitantly with synaptic complex assembly but at a post-synaptic step, when the accessory factor FtsK might be needed to license the reaction by promoting a conformational change.
source: Contrary to previous assumption, bending of the dif sites does not occur concomitantly with synaptic complex assembly but at a post-synaptic step, when the accessory factor FtsK might be needed to license the reaction by promoting a conformational change.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: The structural insights help to better understand how Xer proteins function and how they have adapted the tyrosine recombinase machinery for their unique genome maintenance function.
source: Our structural insights help us to better understand how Xer proteins function and how they have adapted the tyrosine recombinase machinery for their unique genome maintenance function.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the significance of the work.

claim: The data can help to improve XerH-based genetic engineering tools that have been recently introduced for markerless gene deletions in H. pylori.
source: In the long term, our data can also help to improve XerH-based genetic engineering tools that have been recently introduced for markerless gene deletions in H. pylori (Debowski et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential applications of the work, supported by a citation.
